before.label: Roland Barthes
before.description: Analyzes myth as the naturalization of historically produced meanings and studies how historical narratives signify reality. His challenge to authorial closure shifts attention to textual plurality and the reader. Historians and cultural theorists adapt these arguments while disputing their scope.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Mythologies (1957); “The Death of the Author” (1967); S/Z (1970).
before.scope_note: Individual thinker with a changing trajectory, not one fixed structuralist method. Mythologies (1957), Elements of Semiology (1964), the history/authorship essays (1967), The Reality Effect (1968) and S/Z (1970) are distinct works. Saussure, Jakobson, Kristeva, Nietzsche, Marx and Vernant are named resources with different scopes. Bann questions the implied decline of historians’ concern with reality; Hebdige makes a particular style-analysis adaptation. Rhetorical effects do not alone establish that events are imaginary, and the theoretical reader is not a biography of actual readers. S/Z and later photographic inquiry await bounded primary reading; the clinical analogies and sweeping historical generalizations remain attributed.

before.label: Jacques Lacan
before.description: Rereads Freud through identification, language and symbolic relations. The mirror-stage argument explains ego unity through an external image; later work recasts dream condensation and displacement through metaphor and metonymy. His divided subject becomes a resource and a problem for historical accounts of gender.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Freud is a fundamental antecedent; Saussure, Jakobson, and Lévi-Strauss inform Lacan’s approach. Écrits (1966).
before.scope_note: Individual thinker, not a uniform school. The 1949 mirror-stage paper, 1953 report first published in 1956, 1957 linguistic essay and 1966 Écrits collection are distinct witnesses. Saussure’s diagram is transformed, Jakobson explicitly credited, and Lévi-Strauss named as a resource. Althusser appropriates his reading of Freud; Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but questions universal sexual antagonism and limited historical variability. These are situated theoretical arguments, not independently established clinical or developmental facts. Later seminars and revisions remain outside this bounded primary reading.

before.label: Historical epistemology
before.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in1943.
before.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

before.label: Michel Foucault
before.description: Studies how objects of knowledge and subjects take shape through historically specific practices. Archaeology examines discursive formations; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Power works through actions upon possible actions, with institutions, resistance and changing forms of subjectivity entering the analysis.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Order of Things (1966); Discipline and Punish (1975); History of Sexuality I (1976). His association with structuralism is contested.
before.scope_note: Individual thinker with changing projects, not a uniform structuralist school. History of Madness (1961), archaeological inquiry, genealogy and the 1982 account of subjects are distinct contexts. Canguilhem and Nietzsche supply named resources. Derrida’s challenge and Foucault’s reply concern reason, madness, Descartes and discursive practice; neither settles their whole relationship. Historians including Scott, Chartier, Goldstein, Said and Stoler adapt and criticize different aspects, with separately scoped evidence. Comparative historical generalizations remain attributed. Later ethics and self-practice require further bounded primary reading.

before.label: Critical historical scholarship
before.description: Source criticism and historical particularity develop through many traditions: philology, antiquarian research, ecclesiastical scholarship, archives, and university seminars. Ranke is a major exemplar, not their sole origin. Its approaches distinguish documentary authenticity, language and meaning, historical questions, and interpretation of conditions; these operations can support political, social and cultural subjects.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886); archival practice spreads far beyond political and diplomatic subjects. This tradition is not simply synonymous with positivism.

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

before.label: Historical materialism
before.description: Modes of production, relations of exploitation, class struggle, and historically specific capitalism. Later Marxists disagree over determinism, agency, and culture. Marx’s 1859 developmental propositions coexist with his 1877 rejection of a universal path. Later debates concern political action, imperial accumulation, dialectical and analytical explanation, and reproduction of material life.

strands.title: Political struggle and economic determination

strands.works: Accumulation of Capital, chapter 31 (1913); Imperialism, 1920 preface

before.label: Interpretive historical sociology
before.description: Interpretive understanding, ideal types, legitimate domination, rationalization, and comparative histories of capitalism and religion. before.scope_note: Interpretive sociology, capitalist development, and theories of domination travel through different readers and intermediaries. Weber’s qualified defense of materialist inquiry prevents a simple Marx-versus-ideas binary.

strands.title: Meaning and causal evidence

strands.title: Ideal types and collective action
strands.focus: Types clarify comparison without serving as averages or compulsory stages. States and organizations matter through actions and meaningful orientations; methodological individualism does not entail individualistic political values.

strands.title: Value relevance and public validity
strands.focus: Cultural concerns select questions; this does not make the validity of answers arbitrary. General regularities help explain particular histories but cannot alone supply a complete account of a specific constellation.

before.label: Historical economics
before.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction. Earlier disputes also separate Jones’s comparative tenures, Roscher’s contextual programme, Hildebrand’s critique of opposed specialization schemes and Knies’s objections to Roscher’s method. Leslie’s account emphasizes policy differences within historical inquiry.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Gustav Schmoller; William Ashley; William Cunningham; Arnold Toynbee. Thorold Rogers supplies a related empirical tradition in prices and wages. Contextual readings now distinguish Roscher’s 1843 programme, Schmoller’s 1883 methodological review, Cunningham’s textbook, Ashley’s medieval studies, Toynbee’s lectures, Rogers’s wage research and Menger’s criticism.

before.scope_note: German historical economics, British institutional history, and empirical price studies overlap without forming one school. Roscher’s earlier programme and Schmoller’s generation differ. Menger is shown as a critic, and Toynbee explicitly rejects exclusive reliance on historical investigation. National and civilizational categories in these texts are historical claims to examine, not a globally representative framework. Jones’s providential harmony and Hildebrand’s national-capacity judgments are not adopted as findings.

before.scope_note: Classical political economy and neoclassical modelling have different chronologies; North’s later institutional revisions add another distinction. This selection foregrounds earlier resources for historical inquiry, not a complete history of twentieth-century economics. Mill’s institutional argument and Marshall’s qualified assumptions prevent a blanket equation of theory with timeless laws. Polanyi appears as a later critic of a specific classical account, extending the selection’s historical reception without turning it into a complete history of twentieth-century theory. Earlier resources remain central, now joined by selected twentieth-century historical uses: Furtado’s Keynes reference, Block/Somers’s Polanyi reception and Lipset’s Schumpeter definition. These do not constitute comprehensive coverage of modern economics. Mill’s property qualifications coexist with colonial and civilizational assumptions; Marx’s Wakefield critique also retains a settler frame. Naoroji adds an Indian appropriation of Mill, not a globally representative roster.

before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. Driver examines the practices and disagreements of imperial geographical inquiry. Sauer’s historical reconstruction, Cosgrove’s criticism of visual neutrality and Febvre’s geographical collaborations reveal further disagreements within landscape inquiry.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Paul Vidal de la Blache influences Febvre and Bloch; George Perkins Marsh, Man and Nature (1864), is an environmental precursor, not an Annales founder. Additional readings: Sauer, “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949).

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

strands.title: Human activity and regional individuality

strands.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

strands.focus: Marsh brings historical human action into inquiry about forests, waters and land; later historians recognize this precursor.
strands.works: Man and Nature (1864)

strands.title: Physical and cultural landscape forms
strands.focus: Sauer examines associations of landscape forms and their histories, resisting a rigid physical determinism.
strands.works: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925)

strands.title: Ecological observation and landscape reading
strands.focus: Leopold’s observation and teaching connect ecological processes with human conduct; Cronon recalls a specific teaching inheritance.
strands.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949); Cronon’s retrospective afterword

strands.title: Human ecology and medical geography
strands.focus: Sorre’s project supplies a named geographical resource for conceptual inquiry.
strands.works: Les fondements biologiques (1943)

strands.title: Mobility and unequal power
strands.focus: Massey asks who moves, who controls movement and how gender and colonial histories differentiate experience.
strands.works: A Global Sense of Place (1991)

strands.title: Place, tradition and historical change
strands.focus: Massey disputes the necessary association of place identity with fixed tradition; Harvey allows valuable local resistance while questioning its sufficiency.

strands.title: Geographical resources in public history
strands.focus: Hayden uses Harvey while citing Massey’s feminist criticism in a project joining urban landscapes and public memory.
strands.works: The Power of Place (1995)

strands.title: Imperial networks and contested observation
strands.focus: Driver examines conflicting standards, instruments and observer credibility; colonial support did not make all geographical knowledge uniform.
strands.works: Geography’s Empire (1992); Hints to Travellers article (issue 1998)

strands.title: Reconstructing changing cultural landscapes
strands.focus: Sauer proposes reconstructing past cultural landscapes and their succession. His organic analogy is a working method rather than a literal biological law; claims of neutral observation and culture cycles remain open to criticism.
strands.works: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925), reprint 326–327, 333, 342–344

strands.title: Landscape as a historically situated way of seeing
strands.focus: Cosgrove explicitly challenges the neutrality of the areal concept and links visual conventions with property and power. His criticism of static chorology is placed beside Sauer’s own reconstruction of change, preserving disagreement.
strands.works: Cosgrove (1985), 56–59; Sauer (1925), reprint 343–344

strands.title: Historical inquiry, geographical resources and criticism
strands.focus: Vidal supplies methodological resources to Febvre; Sion encourages the project and Bataillon contributes notes. Sauer praises its criticism of environmentalism but questions its representation of geographical thought.
strands.works: La Terre et l’évolution humaine (1922); Sauer (1925); Febvre’s retrospective Combats essay

strands.title: Collaborative place history
strands.focus: The 1995 spatial-history section includes Rita and Jackie Huggins with Jane M. Jacobs. Verified coauthorship and the public finding aid document collaboration; detailed article interpretation remains limited by access.
strands.works: Kooramindanjie: Place and the Postcolonial (1995)

strands.title: Dispersed farming as historical geography
strands.focus: Hewes’s suitcase-farming study is used in later agricultural environmental explanation; shared citation does not settle disagreements about capitalism, farming or government.
strands.works: The Suitcase-Farming Frontier (1973), cited in Worster (1986) and discussed by McDean (1986)

Literary experiments and editorial selection also supply resources for later historical methods.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes (1841); Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918). Biography does not originate with either writer.

before.scope_note: Earlier roots and literary practices overlap with modern historical biography without forming one origin story. Plutarch is one ancient example; Johnson’s private lives precede Carlyle’s Heroes. Strachey names particular models and sources, and Woolf distinguishes his achievements and failures. Her English canon is not a universal history of biography. Translations and abridgments mediate the texts encountered here; named literary resources do not by themselves establish a school’s founding.

strands.title: Private particulars, conversation and narrative

strands.title: Creative individuals and historical belief

strands.title: Compact portraits and acknowledged models
strands.focus: Strachey chooses concentrated portraits, invokes French eloges and uses Cook’s research. Selection is a stated artistic procedure, not representative sampling of the whole age.
strands.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface and postscript

strands.title: Checkable evidence and invention
strands.focus: Woolf’s contrasting judgments of Strachey’s royal biographies test how documentary limits constrain imaginative form. Her conclusions remain criticism, not a settled law of biography.
strands.works: The Art of Biography (1939)

strands.title: Discontinuous narration and the coherent self
strands.focus: Levi and Bourdieu use named literary experiments to question retrospective coherence. The novels are resources for later arguments, not automatic origins of historical schools.
strands.works: Levi (1989); Bourdieu (1986), cited literary examples

before.label: Strategic & military scholarship
before.description: Brings strategic reasoning, critical campaign scholarship and the editing of military texts into view. Clausewitz, Jomini, Delbrück, Mahan, Corbett and the translated Sun Tzu tradition pose different questions about judgment, evidence and the purposes of war. Professional education and academic inquiry overlap without being identical.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832); Hans Delbrück joins source criticism to analysis of warfare.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Proposes explaining sea power within general history and its social, political and economic surroundings. His naval-professional perspective and selected Europe/America scope are explicit.
representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Treats naval operations within wider maritime coordination of armies, fleets and political purposes. Theory aids education and deliberation; this is a situated British imperial perspective.
representative_people.works: Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction

representative_people.context: Organizes posthumous publication and describes intellectual companionship and assistance from others. Her modest prefatory disclaimer does not make editorial work intellectually empty.
representative_people.works: Preface to On War, 30 June 1832

representative_people.context: Defends strategic principles while insisting that war also turns on morale, judgment and contingencies. His conclusion qualifies a wholly mechanical characterization.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Mendell/Craighill translation (1862), conclusion

representative_people.context: Traditional attribution of a Chinese strategic text that prioritizes overcoming resistance and preserving forces over repeated destructive combat. Neither a fixed composition date nor a uniform Chinese tradition is asserted.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), chapter III §§1–8

representative_people.context: Makes translation, paragraph arrangement and selective Chinese commentary part of the English text’s reception; his criticism of predecessors remains a contested editorial judgment.
representative_people.works: The Art of War (1910), translator’s preface and commentary

representative_people.context: Proposes and collaborates with Howard on a new Clausewitz translation. Strachan later assesses its modernization; translating does not simply transmit an unchanged meaning.
representative_people.works: With Michael Howard, On War (1976), translation; collaboration documented by Strachan

representative_people.context: Challenges Keegan’s culture/politics opposition while valuing The Face of Battle. Later web corrections are distinguished from the original polemic.
representative_people.works: “John Keegan and the Grand Tradition of Trashing Clausewitz” (1994)

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Paret on translating Clausewitz; readable modern vocabulary is also an object of later interpretive criticism.
representative_people.works: With Peter Paret, On War (1976), translation

representative_people.context: Questions Clausewitz through a cultural account of warfare, as represented in Bassford’s opposing reception. This is distinct from the combat-reconstruction method of his earlier book.
representative_people.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated by Bassford (1994)

representative_people.context: Delbrück explicitly credits demographic groundwork while correcting individual estimates. A named methodological resource, not acceptance of every army figure.
representative_people.works: Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886), acknowledged in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

before.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. after.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. before.label: Economic history
before.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000).

representative_people.context: Treats institutions, law and custom as part of economic explanation; his dispute with Menger concerns how abstraction should proceed.
representative_people.works: “Zur Methodologie der Staats- und Sozialwissenschaften” (1883; English translation 2021)

representative_people.context: Agrarian reconstruction tests legal and economic explanations against regional and documentary differences; religion/capitalism adds ethical and causal questions.
representative_people.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926)

representative_people.context: Combines medieval institutional research with personal reconstruction; distinguishes kinds of evidence and acknowledges editorial and documentary collaboration.

after.label: Economic history
after.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
after.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000).

before.label: Military history
before.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Combines campaign reconstruction, wider social context and war-studies teaching. Archival loss/access constrained the 1961 study; later Ultra disclosure exposed limits of official Grand Strategy records.
representative_people.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); Grand Strategy, IV (1972); War in European History (1976)

representative_people.context: Studies combat experience through critically assessed testimony, documents and physical possibility. representative_people.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available opening excerpt; A History of Warfare (1993), separate argument mediated by Bassford

representative_people.context: Studies bodily injury, disease and masculinity in Britain during and after the Great War.

before.label: Political history
before.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

before.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. Bourdieu questions narrated coherence without banning life histories; Levi emphasizes choices within constraints and investigates group formation. Biography can explain wider relations, but its scale and source gaps remain subjects of criticism. Non-European traditions and original translation witnesses require further research; the current selection is not exhaustive.

after.scope_note: A genre and set of methods with ancient and varied roots, not inherently great-man history, psychohistory or microstoria. The selected roster combines earlier practices, modern historical work and critics. Davis’s comparison preserves religious and colonial differences; her imagined prologue is not historical testimony. before.label: History of science
before.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
before.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

before.label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
before.description: Groups related arguments for historical specificity and interpretive understanding. German Historismus and British and Italian idealism are not one doctrine: Collingwood’s re-enactment is a particular account of historical thought, not a method shared by everyone here. This usage differs from Popper’s criticism of predictive laws of historical development. Approaches separate documentary interpretation, the human sciences, living historical questions, developmental individuality and rethinking past arguments; their disagreements concern evidence, values, political power and historical context.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Wilhelm Dilthey; Benedetto Croce, Theory and History of Historiography (1917); Friedrich Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936); R. G. Collingwood, The Idea of History (1946, posthumous).

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Studies individuality and development in a selected genealogy of historicism. His account of national statehood and power receives a specific, attributed criticism from Paddock; neither the definition nor the criticism represents every historicism.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through publisher and scholarly selections

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Combines interpretive understanding with a critical method and a conception of the moral historical world. His approach bridges documentary scholarship and philosophical reflection without becoming identical to Dilthey or Croce.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted 1893 English translation)

representative_people.context: Provides an earlier comparison for historical individuality and the value of epochs. His theology and documentary practice differ from later philosophies; no backward influence is implied.
representative_people.works: 1824 preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
representative_people.works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
representative_people.works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

representative_people.context: A resource in Dilthey’s expanded critical perspective and an author central to Meinecke’s selective genealogy. These distinct receptions do not establish one unbroken school.
representative_people.works: Historical philosophy; Meinecke’s Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock’s account

representative_people.context: An explicitly documented recipient of Collingwood’s question/answer logic, with substantial analytical-philosophical commitments. Placement records selective reception and does not label the Cambridge approach idealist.
representative_people.works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969), reception discussed in the 2002 interview

before.scope_note: German historicism, Italian idealism, and Collingwood’s re-enactment are not one doctrine; neither is this Popper’s usage of historicism.

strands.title: Understanding through historical investigation

strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected sections

strands.title: Human sciences, theory and practical judgment
strands.focus: The 1883 program distinguishes historical assertions, theoretical uniformities and evaluations/rules. Its broad remit includes humanities and social sciences, rather than forbidding every explanatory generalization.
strands.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2 and 6

strands.title: Expressions and shared historical worlds
strands.focus: Later Dilthey situates understanding in meaningful expressions, institutions and common historical life. Hegel’s objective spirit is appropriated with different commitments; individual introspection is insufficient.
strands.works: Formation of the Historical World (1910) and related drafts, through editors and SEP

strands.title: Present questions and preserved records
strands.focus: Croce distinguishes historical thinking from preserved chronicle without rejecting preservation. His explicit engagement with Droysen joins appreciation to criticism of abstract source categories.
strands.works: Theory & History of Historiography, I.1

strands.title: Individuality, development and state power
strands.focus: Meinecke’s genealogy privileges historical development and particularity. Paddock challenges its treatment of national statehood and supposed breaks in the author’s outlook; that is an attributed interpretation based on selected passages.
strands.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), mediated readings

strands.title: Re-enactment, context and changing questions
strands.focus: Rethinking an argument differs from reliving its sensations. Skinner’s particular reception stresses questions and answers while drawing heavily on analytical philosophy; this is not the shared method of everyone in the umbrella.
strands.works: The Idea of History, Epilegomena §4; An Autobiography through Skinner’s interview

before.label: Helen Maud Cam
before.date_label: Medieval institutions, law, and local evidence · interwar–postwar
before.description: Reconstructs medieval government through local institutions, legal records and parliamentary representation. Her research examines the making and editing of evidence as well as the relations between communities and central authority. Her contribution also includes teaching, scholarly editing and histories of historians.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944); studies of legal and constitutional history. IHR identifies local sources and medieval political history as central to her work.
before.scope_note: Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921) and later collections distinguish documents from the institutions they disclose. Cam’s 1948 Stubbs opening combines appreciation with revision; Cheney identifies Maitland, Vinogradoff and documentary training, while questioning some juristic deductions and larger claims of legal progress. His memoir is a situated assessment, not a substitute for her full cases. Women’s place in scholarship is not confined to women’s-history subjects; the Ranke comparison remains undirected.

before.label: Marc Bloch
before.description: Comparative historian of social relations, sacred kingship and historical evidence. His Apologie distinguishes causes from beginnings and interrogates traces through questions, using present observation without collapsing historical differences.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Royal Touch (1924); Feudal Society (1939–40).
before.scope_note: The Royal Touch and Feudal Society provide distinct historical objects; the unfinished, posthumously published Apologie (1949) addresses method. Pirenne, Maitland and Simiand appear as specific resources, not interchangeable schools. Primary methodological passages are checked; the historical books retain narrower description/metadata support and unresolved questions about generalization.

before.label: Lucien Febvre
before.description: Problem-led historian of geography, belief and socially organized feelings, and collaborator in book history. He challenges anachronistic ideas about Rabelais, critically adapts cultural and psychological resources, and prompts both productive reception and objections.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century (1942).
before.scope_note: The Unbelief polemic (1942), sensitivity essay (1941) and Febvre–Martin book project are distinct inquiries. Historical conditions of thought should not become an unquestioned assertion that dissent was impossible. Walker’s appreciative criticism preserves that dispute. Wallon and Blondel are specific psychological resources; Martin’s substantial drafting and research are separately credited.

before.label: Fernand Braudel
before.description: Historian of multiple durations, material life, markets and capitalism. His models require historical testing and have finite lifespans. He borrows from Lévi-Strauss, engages Wallerstein and criticizes Weber’s explanation of capitalist origins.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Mediterranean (1949); “Histoire et sciences sociales: La longue durée” (1958).
before.scope_note: The Mediterranean (1949), the duration essay (1958) and the 1977 economic synthesis have distinct objects. Febvre’s commission and Labrousse’s conjunctures are named resources. Braudel’s market/capitalism distinction permits overlap; his Weber polemic and differing world-economy chronology remain attributed positions. Chartier later questions his hierarchy of explanation. Selected methodological and economic passages are checked; the Mediterranean monograph is not newly read in full.

before.label: Ernest Labrousse
before.description: Investigates differential prices, incomes and conjunctures to explain social tensions and revolutionary crises. His collective inquiry recognizes uneven sectoral movements; later historians debate the construction of his evidence and the conditions of his causal model.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Studies of prices, incomes, and the crisis of the ancien régime.
before.scope_note: Esquisse (1933), the unfinished La Crise (1944) and “Panoramas de la crise” (1956) are distinct projects. Simiand and Hamilton are retrospectively identified resources; Braudel’s appreciative use includes reservations about short duration. Perrot’s supervised strike research combines serial training with attention to lived action. Primary 1956 opening and selected scholarly reception are checked; full monographs, interview body and later mathematical defense remain unread.

before.label: Maurice Dobb
before.description: Explains capitalist development through changing production relations and class conflict, while allowing trade to interact with those relations. His historical synthesis prompts international debate over feudalism, labour, the state and accumulation.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946).
before.scope_note: Studies (1946) and the 1950 reply to Sweezy are distinct texts. The reply explicitly uses Marx, Tawney and other historians; it concedes weak evidence for one accumulation hypothesis. Sweezy challenges definition and regional transfer; Takahashi adds a Japanese intervention focused on Western Europe. The primary reply is read in full, not the monograph or all later comparisons. His Asia and historical-stage claims remain attributed positions.

before.label: Rodney Hilton
before.description: Examines medieval peasant society, collective action and class relations through comparative historical inquiry. Economic conditions interact with political organization and belief; his study of 1381 distinguishes defeat, limited gains and longer-term consequences.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Studies of medieval peasantries and debates over the transition from feudalism.
before.scope_note: Bond Men Made Free (1973) names Bloch and several economic historians as resources; specific Power/Duby criticisms coexist with productive exchange. Contemporary Genet criticism questions period and state differentiation. Selected primary passages reveal mediation and limits on transferring medieval conclusions to other times; full case evidence is not independently audited. Birrell, Dyer, Hill and Razi are explicitly credited draft readers, not inferred coauthors.

before.label: Dona Torr
before.description: Combines labour biography, translation, annotation, tutoring and collaborative historical publication. Her work connects individual lives with radical political traditions, while testimony and criticism reveal differences over interpretation, group organization and party commitments.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Tom Mann and His Times; Historians’ Group projects.
before.scope_note: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956), was prepared with help from Hill and Morton; the second volume remained unfinished, with fragments later edited by E. P. Thompson. Archive descriptions distinguish drafts from published chapters. Editions of Marx/Engels provide another form of intellectual contribution. Murphy’s contemporary review challenges biographical framing. Primary testimony/review and archival descriptions are checked; the original monograph, notebooks and translations are not read in full.

before.label: Eric Hobsbawm
before.description: Studies labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and national identifications across different scales. Cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis coexist; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Labouring Men (1964); with Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); response to Stone on narrative (1980).
before.scope_note: The 1980 narrative reply, Bandits in its revised 2000 form, and Nations and Nationalism (1990/1992) distinguish debate, self-revision and historical synthesis. Later concessions about myth and political power are not projected into 1969. Colombian interlocutors and European comparative models supply named resources. Labouring Men and the main nationalism cases remain unread; selected primary support does not audit his entire career or generalizations.

before.label: Christopher Hill
before.description: Examines the English Revolution through social conflict, religious arguments and unrealized radical alternatives. His changing projects and exchanges with collaborators and critics expose questions about evidence, categories and comparative explanation.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972).
before.scope_note: The original 1940 pamphlet, its 1955 revision preface and The World Turned Upside Down (1972) are distinct. Hill credits Dobb, Hilton, Yates and other resources; a 1986 review values Barg’s Soviet comparisons. The Ranter debate distinguishes organized sect, milieu and hostile labeling, with disagreement on several sides. Introductions and selected exchanges are read; the full cases, Davis’s monograph and Hill’s later response remain follow-ups.

before.label: R. H. Tawney
before.description: Relates agrarian institutions, economic change and religious ethics through historically differentiated inquiry. His acknowledged debts coexist with criticism of one-sided explanations and attention to the limits of documentary and statistical evidence.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926); with Eileen Power, Tudor Economic Documents (1924).
before.scope_note: The Agrarian Problem (1912) and Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926) address related but distinct problems. Ashley, Weber and named agrarian historians provide resources; Tawney’s Weber criticism concerns causal weight and religious differences. Dobb’s reception does not make Tawney a Marxist. Preface, introduction and selected notes/concluding passages are checked; detailed cases and the later 1936 preface remain unread. Tutorial discussion and credited research assistance belong to the work’s production.

before.label: Roger Chartier
before.description: Explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation.
before.representative_figures_and_works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989).
before.scope_note: The 1989 article explicitly engages McKenzie, Ricœur, Fish, Marin, Durkheim/Mauss, Elias, Ginzburg, Certeau and Foucault. Productive Foucault use coexists with a different account of appropriation; criticism of Braudel concerns an explanatory hierarchy. Social divisions include gender, generation, religion and education as well as class. The primary article is checked, but its cited works and historical examples do not thereby receive independent verification.
